c.tagline: Mexico's Pacific 'sailfish capital' of twin bays, golden beaches and a busy port.

taxi.fareNote: Manzanillo taxis are unmetered and priced by zone, so agree the fare before setting off; Uber and DiDi both operate and usually give a cheaper upfront price.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

hood_landmark.Centro (Downtown / Zona Centro): Pez Vela (sailfish) monument, Zona Centro Manzanillo

avoid.reason: Stay within the beach, hotel and port zones — the rest of Colima state is under do-not-travel advisories for cartel violence.
Don't leave valuables on the beach, avoid deserted stretches after dark, and skip intercity road travel at night.

hood_desc: Manzanillo's working downtown wrapped around the port and the Jardin Alvaro Obregon plaza, with the giant blue Pez Vela (sailfish) monument, seafood cocktail stands and the cheapest local hotels; best for budget travelers who want authentic port-city life.

A long sandy spit between downtown and the bays lined with mid-range hotels and restaurants on Playa Las Brisas; a convenient, good-value base close to the beach and a short drive from both the center and Santiago.
A busy commercial neighborhood at the crossroads between the two bays with supermarkets, restaurants and everyday services; practical and central for longer stays, though not a beach hood itself.
The upscale peninsula dividing Manzanillo and Santiago bays, home to the landmark Moorish-white Las Hadas resort, Playa La Audiencia and marinas; best for a resort splurge with calm swimming coves.

A relaxed residential-resort area on Santiago Bay's north shore with the wide Playa Miramar (the area's best swimming and surf beach), gated communities and vacation rentals; suits families and surfers wanting a quiet beach stay.
lodging: Best Western Plus Luna del Mar

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: Local buses and colectivos run roughly 5:00am to 10:00pm along the bay corridor between downtown, Salagua and Santiago; taxis and ride apps fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Manzanillo has no metro, tram, or rail transit; getting around this spread-out port city means the cheap urban buses and colectivos that run the Manzanillo-Santiago corridor, taxis, or ride-hailing apps, and a car is handy for reaching the outer beaches.
transit.pay: City buses and colectivos are paid in cash to the driver (roughly MXN 10-15 a ride); there is no rechargeable transit card. Taxis are unmetered, so agree the fare first.

bus: Central de Autobuses Manzanillo (main intercity bus terminal)

transit.m: Uber/DiDi to the bays (Santiago/Las Brisas), ~30-40 min
Authorized airport taxi/van to Manzanillo, ~35-45 min

tip.r: Around 10-15% at restaurants is customary; rounding up for taxis and leaving small change for hotel and bar staff is appreciated.

food.name: Ceviche de Pez Vela Estilo Colima
food.desc: Finely minced sailfish cured in lime with carrot, onion and chile, pressed dry and piled on crisp tostadas; Colima's own style of ceviche.

places.name: Mariscos Carlos
places.note: Named among Manzanillo's top three seafood places for a decade; the ceviche is the order to make.

places.name: La Bichi
places.note: Specialises in fish tacos and ceviche with notably fresh product at moderate prices.

places.name: Mariscos Dona Concha
places.note: Long-standing local marisqueria that regularly tops city seafood lists.

food.name: Pescado Zarandeado
food.desc: Whole butterflied snapper or dorado rubbed with chile and achiote, then grilled in a wire basket over wood until smoky.

places.name: El Indio
places.note: Beachfront palapa on Miramar where the grill runs all afternoon; toes-in-the-sand seating.

places.name: Mariscos La Huerta
places.note: Casual open-air spot with beach views and unpretentious grilled fish at fair prices.

places.name: El Cihuateco
places.note: Neighborhood marisqueria on the Santiago side, popular with local families for grilled whole fish.

food.name: Camarones al Mojo de Ajo
food.desc: Pacific shrimp seared in butter and heaps of sliced garlic, served with rice and warm tortillas; the coconut-crusted version is equally local.

places.name: Mariscos Carlos
places.note: Its garlic shrimp and bean-filled tacos dorados are the dishes regulars come back for.

places.name: Mariscos El Camaron
places.note: Reliable, well-reviewed shrimp house serving the classic garlic and chipotle preparations.

places.name: Restaurante Las Brisas
places.note: Family-friendly spot rated for coconut shrimp, fish tacos and reasonable prices.

food.name: Tatemado de Colima
food.desc: Pork slow-braised in dried chile and coconut vinegar until dark and sticky, the defining fiesta dish of Colima state.

places.name: Los Naranjos
places.note: Downtown institution serving Colima home cooking rather than tourist seafood.

places.name: Restaurant Chantilly
places.note: Landmark cafe on the main square, a fixture for regional plates and breakfast for decades.

places.name: Mercado Municipal fondas
places.note: Market kitchens cook tatemado on weekends; ask which fonda has it that day.

food.name: Birria
food.desc: Goat or beef stewed for hours in a chile adobo and served as a soupy bowl with lime, onion and tortillas, eaten mainly at breakfast.

places.name: Mercado Municipal fondas
places.note: Market birria stands open early and sell out by midday; the cheapest honest bowl in town.

places.name: Mercado de Santiago
places.note: Second market on the north side with its own birria and menudo counters.

places.name: Los Naranjos
places.note: Sit-down option for regional stews if you would rather not eat at a market counter.

food.name: Sopitos Colimenses
food.desc: Small thick tortillas fried and topped with shredded pork, cabbage, cheese and a thin tomato broth poured over at the last second.

places.name: Jardin Alvaro Obregon evening stands
places.note: Antojito carts set up around the main plaza after dark, the traditional place to eat sopitos.

places.name: Mercado Municipal fondas
places.note: Daytime market counters serving sopitos, tacos dorados and other Colima antojitos.

places.name: Restaurant Chantilly
places.note: Reliable indoor alternative on the plaza for regional snacks and coffee.

food.name: Tuba
food.desc: Sweet sap tapped from coconut palms, served cold over ice with chopped apple and peanuts; Colima's signature refresher, sold from gourds.

places.name: Tuberos, Jardin Alvaro Obregon
places.note: Vendors carry the tuba in gourds slung on poles and pour it fresh around the plaza.

places.name: Playa Miramar vendors
places.note: Beach tuberos work the sand all afternoon; the version with peanuts and apple is standard.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Market stalls sell tuba by the cup or bottle to take away.

food.name: Tejuino
food.desc: Lightly fermented masa drink with piloncillo, lime and salt, poured over shaved ice and often topped with lime sorbet.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Market carts serve tejuino with a scoop of nieve de limon, the traditional way.

places.name: Jardin Alvaro Obregon carts
places.note: Plaza vendors keep tejuino next to the tuba; both are sold from the same stands.

places.name: Playa Santiago vendors
places.note: Beach carts on the Santiago bay selling tejuino and aguas frescas.

landmarks: El Pez Vela (Giant Sailfish Monument)
Sculptor Sebastián's towering blue sailfish leaps over the downtown plaza, the defiant emblem of a city crowned the world's sailfish capital.
Malecón de Manzanillo
A breezy harborfront promenade of sculptures and pelican-topped pilings where cruise ships, fishing boats and Pacific sunsets share the same frame.
Jardín Álvaro Obregón
Manzanillo's palm-shaded main square beside the port, alive with evening danzón, ice-cream vendors and views of the giant sailfish sculpture.
Playa La Audiencia
A calm, cove-sheltered crescent on the Santiago Peninsula, beloved for gentle swimming, water sports and its backdrop of bougainvillea-draped hills.
Playa Miramar
Santiago Bay's long golden strand draws boogie boarders and horseback riders, with palapa restaurants serving ceviche steps from the surf.
Las Hadas Resort and Marina
The whitewashed Moorish-fantasy resort that starred in the film '10', its minarets and yacht-filled marina remain Manzanillo's most glamorous photo stop.
El Tortugario Ecological Center (Cuyutlán)
A beachside sanctuary near Cuyutlán where visitors release baby sea turtles and cruise mangrove channels thick with birdlife and crocodiles.
Laguna de Cuyutlán
One of Mexico's largest coastal lagoons, its mangrove-lined waters shelter herons, spoonbills and seasonal flocks that thrill birdwatchers on boat tours.
Iguanario de Archundia
A quirky downtown sanctuary where hundreds of green iguanas laze in riverside trees, fed and protected by a devoted local family.
Península de Santiago viewpoints
The rocky headland dividing Manzanillo's twin bays offers cliffside miradors where both sweeping coastlines glow copper at sunset.

train.note: Mexico has no passenger rail service to Manzanillo; the city's rail lines are freight-only, serving one of the country's busiest Pacific cargo ports.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Manzanillo. Frequent first-class coaches (ETN, Primera Plus, Autotransportes del Pacifico) run from the Central de Autobuses to Colima, Guadalajara, Barra de Navidad and Mexico City.

ferry.note: Manzanillo is a major commercial and cruise port but has no scheduled passenger ferry service; the harbor handles cargo ships and seasonal cruise calls.

half.name: Barra de Navidad
half.blurb: Laid-back beach town and lagoon on the Jalisco Costalegre, about 1 hr north up the coast.

half.name: Cuyutlan
half.blurb: Black-sand beach village known for its 'Ola Verde' green wave and the El Tortugario turtle sanctuary, about 45 min south.

half.name: Comala
half.blurb: A white-washed 'Pueblo Magico' of arcaded plazas and ponche liqueur near Colima, about 1.5 hrs inland.

full.name: Colima & Volcan de Colima
full.blurb: The colonial state capital beneath one of Mexico's most active volcanoes, about 1.5 hrs inland.

full.name: Guadalajara
full.blurb: Jalisco's tequila-and-mariachi capital, roughly 3.5-4 hrs northeast by highway.
